cards.front: In randomized grassland experiments, why can a mixture of plant species yield extra and also vary less from year to year?
cards.back: A plot's production is the sum of what its species produce. The sum beats expectation when it exceeds the monoculture-based expected yield, and it steadies because species' swings partly cancel, unless they rise and fall together.
cards.quote: A plot's production is the sum of what its species produce.

cards.front: In a biodiversity experiment, a mixture's expected yield is each species' monoculture yield times its share of the seed; with an even sowing, that is the {{c1::average}} monoculture, not the best.
cards.quote: Expected yield is each species' monoculture yield times its share of the seed; with an even sowing, that is the average monoculture, not the best.

cards.front: What is an ecosystem function? Give an example from a grassland.
cards.back: A rate or stock of a process: for example a field's yearly plant production, the nitrogen it holds, or how fast litter decays.
cards.quote: An ecosystem function is a rate or stock of a process
cards.section: The question: does richness change what an ecosystem does?

cards.front: {{c1::Species richness}} is the number of species present, the simplest measure of diversity.
cards.quote: Species richness is the number of species present, the simplest diversity measure from diversity and succession.
cards.section: The question: does richness change what an ecosystem does?

cards.front: A survey of 20 unmanaged meadows finds that species-rich meadows have more aboveground biomass. Can the survey show that richness raises biomass?
cards.back: No. Moisture or fertility could raise both richness and biomass; such a third variable is a confounder. Only assigning richness experimentally breaks that link.
cards.why: That is why ecologists built communities instead of finding them.
cards.quote: Moisture or fertility could raise both richness and biomass
cards.section: The question: does richness change what an ecosystem does?

cards.front: At Cedar Creek, Minnesota, why was every plot sown with the same seed mass, whatever its species number?
cards.back: So rich plots did not simply get more seed: any biomass difference between richness levels could not come from extra sowing.
cards.quote: so rich plots did not simply get more seed
cards.section: Building communities at random: Cedar Creek and BIODEPTH

cards.front: Cedar Creek drew species at random from a pool of 18. Why does random drawing still not remove the effect of species identity?
cards.back: A richer draw is still more likely to include a very productive species, such as a legume. If that species also gains most relative yield in mixture, the partition records a positive selection effect.
cards.quote: Random draws do not remove species identity: a richer draw is still more likely to include a very productive species, such as a legume.
cards.section: Building communities at random: Cedar Creek and BIODEPTH

cards.front: What did the BIODEPTH experiment, across eight European sites, find about plant species number and aboveground biomass?
cards.back: Across sites, communities assembled with fewer plant species had lower average aboveground biomass.
cards.quote: communities assembled with fewer plant species had lower average aboveground biomass
cards.section: Building communities at random: Cedar Creek and BIODEPTH

cards.front: In a richness experiment with a log-linear biomass decline, dropping from 16 species to 8 lowers average biomass by 40 g per square metre. Predict the loss from 4 species to 2.
cards.back: About 40 g per square metre. On a log-linear relation each halving of species number lowers biomass by a similar step, whatever the starting number.
cards.why: Plotted against the logarithm of species number, biomass falls along a straight line.
cards.quote: each halving of species number lowered biomass by a similar step
cards.section: Building communities at random: Cedar Creek and BIODEPTH

cards.front: In BIODEPTH, did species composition matter at a fixed species number?
cards.back: Yes. At a fixed species number, communities with fewer functional groups (such as grasses, legumes and other herbs) were less productive.
cards.quote: at a fixed species number, communities with fewer functional groups (such as grasses, legumes and other herbs) were less productive.
cards.section: Building communities at random: Cedar Creek and BIODEPTH

cards.front: Contrast complementarity and selection as reasons a plant mixture can out-yield its monocultures.
cards.back: Complementarity: species do better together, through resource partitioning or help such as legumes adding nitrogen. Selection: a random mixture is more likely to include the species best alone, and that species gains most.
cards.quote: In plants, complementarity covers resource partitioning (the niche differences from competition) and help between species, such as legumes adding nitrogen.
cards.section: Splitting the extra yield (worked problem)

cards.front: A species' relative yield (RY) is its yield in mixture, Y, divided by its {{c1::yield alone in monoculture, M}}.
cards.back: Expected RY is its sown proportion; ΔRY is observed RY minus expected.
cards.quote: its relative yield (RY): its yield in mixture, Y, divided by its yield alone in monoculture, M.
cards.section: Splitting the extra yield (worked problem)

cards.front: In the Loreau-Hector partition, net effect (observed mixture yield minus expected) = complementarity + {{c1::selection}}.
cards.back: The split is exact.
cards.quote: The net effect, observed mixture yield minus expected, then splits exactly
cards.section: Splitting the extra yield (worked problem)

cards.front: Even sowing of two species. Monocultures: A = 300, B = 100 g per square metre. Mixture: Y_A = 225, Y_B = 50. Find net, complementarity and selection effects.
cards.why: Selection is positive because the high-monoculture species gained more relative yield.
cards.quote: Complementarity = 2 × 0.375 × 250 = +187.5 g per square metre.
cards.section: Splitting the extra yield (worked problem)

cards.front: In a two-species mixture, both species do better than expected, but the low-yielding species gains more relative yield. What are the signs of complementarity and selection?
cards.back: Complementarity positive (both beat expectation); selection negative (gains went to the species small in monoculture).
cards.quote: Both species did better than expected, so complementarity is positive; the low-yielding B gained more, so selection is negative.
cards.section: Splitting the extra yield (worked problem)

cards.front: Even sowing. Monocultures: A = 400, B = 100 g per square metre. Mixture: Y_A = 250, Y_B = 62.5. Find complementarity and selection.
cards.back: RY_A = 0.625 and RY_B = 0.625, so both ΔRY = 0.125. Complementarity = 2 × 0.125 × 250 = +62.5. No ΔRY deviates from the mean, so selection = 0. Net = 312.5 − 250 = +62.5.
cards.quote: With equal gains (both ΔRY = 0.25), no ΔRY deviates from the mean, so selection = 0 and all 125 is complementarity.
cards.section: Splitting the extra yield (worked problem)

cards.front: Species A makes 300 of a two-species mixture's 400 g per square metre, yet the selection effect is negative. Did A fail to dominate?
cards.back: No. A dominates the biomass, but selection asks whether the relative-yield gains went to the species big in monoculture. They went to the other species, so selection is negative.
cards.quote: but selection asks whether the relative-yield gains went to the species big in monoculture
cards.section: Splitting the extra yield (worked problem)

cards.front: Even sowing. Monocultures: A = 400, B = 100 g per square metre. Mixture: Y_A = 120, Y_B = 100. Mean ΔRY is positive. Does the mixture yield extra?
cards.back: No. ΔRY_A = −0.2, ΔRY_B = +0.5, mean 0.15. Complementarity = 2 × 0.15 × 250 = +75; selection = −105. Net = 220 − 250 = −30.
cards.why: Mean ΔRY above zero does not guarantee extra yield; negative selection can outweigh positive complementarity.
cards.quote: had A made 120 and B 100, complementarity would be +75 but selection −105, and the mixture's 220 would miss the expected 250.
cards.section: Splitting the extra yield (worked problem)

cards.front: A mixture that beats its best monoculture, not just the average, shows {{c1::transgressive overyielding}}.
cards.quote: Beating the best monoculture, not just the average, is transgressive overyielding
cards.section: Splitting the extra yield (worked problem)

cards.front: An evenly sown two-species mixture yields 450 g per square metre. Its monocultures yield 500 and 200. Find the net effect and say whether it overyields transgressively.
cards.back: Expected = (500 + 200)/2 = 350, so net = +100: it overyields against the average. It is below the best monoculture (500), so it is not transgressive overyielding.
cards.quote: Beating the best monoculture, not just the average, is transgressive overyielding
cards.section: Splitting the extra yield (worked problem)

cards.front: What did the Loreau-Hector partition show when applied to BIODEPTH?
cards.back: Complementarity was positive overall; selection averaged zero and ranged from negative to positive among sites.
cards.quote: Applied to BIODEPTH, the complementarity effect was positive overall, while the selection effect averaged zero and ranged from negative to positive among sites.
cards.section: Splitting the extra yield (worked problem)

cards.front: A grass-legume experiment reports a large positive complementarity effect. A student concludes the species partition soil nitrogen by rooting depth. Evaluate.
cards.back: Untested. The partition is exact algebra on yields; resource partitioning, legume nitrogen or reduced pathogen pressure could each produce positive complementarity. The rooting-depth idea needs its own test.
cards.quote: A positive complementarity term does not prove resource partitioning: the partition is exact algebra on yields, and legume nitrogen or reduced pathogen pressure could produce it too.
cards.section: Splitting the extra yield (worked problem)

cards.front: What data does the Loreau-Hector partition need?
cards.back: Species-level yields in both the mixtures and the monocultures.
cards.quote: It needs species-level yields in both mixtures and monocultures.
cards.section: Splitting the extra yield (worked problem)

cards.front: Temporal stability of a community is the mean of total biomass across years, μ, divided by its {{c1::standard deviation, σ}}.
cards.quote: Temporal stability is the mean of total community biomass across years, μ ("mu"), divided by its standard deviation, σ ("sigma").
cards.section: Stability: how to score it, and when cancelling fails

cards.front: Distinguish resistance from resilience for an ecosystem function such as production during a drought.
cards.back: Resistance: how little the function changes during the disturbance. Resilience: how fully or quickly it returns afterwards.
cards.quote: Resistance is how little a function changes during a disturbance such as a drought.
cards.section: Stability: how to score it, and when cancelling fails

cards.front: Each species has a mean of 50 g per square metre and a standard deviation of 25, and all are uncorrelated. Find μ/σ of the total for 16 species.
cards.back: μ = 16 × 50 = 800. Variance = 16 × 625 = 10,000, so σ = 100. μ/σ = 8 (versus 2 for one species).
cards.why: Stability grows with the square root of species number when swings are uncorrelated.
cards.quote: Stability grows with the square root of species number (16 species give 8), with no species any steadier.
cards.section: Stability: how to score it, and when cancelling fails

cards.front: Four uncorrelated species each have standard deviation 25. Why is the total's standard deviation 50, not 100?
cards.back: Standard deviations do not add; variances do, when species are uncorrelated. 4 × 625 = 2,500, whose square root is 50.
cards.quote: standard deviations do not add; variances (squared standard deviations) do, when the species are uncorrelated.
cards.section: Stability: how to score it, and when cancelling fails

cards.front: Four species, each mean 50 and standard deviation 25, rise and fall in lockstep (correlation +1). Find μ/σ of the total and compare with one species.
cards.back: Each pair's covariance = 1 × 25 × 25 = 625; six pairs. Variance = 4 × 625 + 2 × 6 × 625 = 10,000, σ = 100. μ/σ = 200/100 = 2, the same as one species: no averaging gain.
cards.why: Variance of a total = sum of variances + twice every pair's covariance.
cards.quote: In general, the variance of a total is the sum of the species' variances plus twice the covariance of every pair
cards.section: Stability: how to score it, and when cancelling fails

cards.front: Two species, each mean 50 and standard deviation 25, have a correlation of −0.5. Find μ/σ of the total and compare with uncorrelated species.
cards.why: Negative correlations cancel more than independent swings.
cards.quote: Negative correlations cancel more: one species rising as another falls is compensatory dynamics.
cards.section: Stability: how to score it, and when cancelling fails

cards.front: One species rising as another falls, a negative correlation that steadies the total, is called {{c1::compensatory dynamics}}.
cards.quote: Negative correlations cancel more: one species rising as another falls is compensatory dynamics.
cards.section: Stability: how to score it, and when cancelling fails

cards.front: What did Tilman, Reich and Knops conclude made Cedar Creek's richer plots steadier from year to year?
cards.back: Statistical averaging and overyielding, not a covariance effect: they found no evidence of one. The 16-species plots averaged 180 percent more biomass than monocultures, and a higher mean raises μ/σ.
cards.quote: At Cedar Creek, Tilman, Reich and Knops found no evidence of a covariance effect.
cards.section: Stability: how to score it, and when cancelling fails

cards.front: Over several years, monoculture plots average 150 g per square metre (standard deviation 50); mixtures average 240 (standard deviation 40). Compare temporal stability.
cards.back: Monocultures: 150/50 = 3. Mixtures: 240/40 = 6. Mixtures are twice as stable, from both a higher mean and a smaller swing.
cards.quote: Temporal stability is the mean of total community biomass across years, μ ("mu"), divided by its standard deviation, σ ("sigma").
cards.section: Stability: how to score it, and when cancelling fails

cards.front: Low-diversity plots produce 300 g per square metre normally, 180 in a drought, 300 the next year. High-diversity plots: 400, 340, 400. What do the data show?
cards.back: Diversity raised resistance (40 percent loss versus 15 percent) but not recovery: both returned fully a year later.
cards.why: Resistance and resilience are separate measures and need not move together.
cards.quote: Resistance is how little a function changes during a disturbance such as a drought.
cards.section: Stability: how to score it, and when cancelling fails

cards.front: Across 46 grassland diversity experiments (Isbell and colleagues, 2015), how did diversity relate to response to wet or dry climate events?
cards.back: Productivity changed about 50 percent at one or two species versus about 25 percent at 16 to 32: greater resistance. No dependence of recovery on diversity was detected a year later.
cards.quote: Yet by one year after each event, they detected no dependence of recovery on diversity.
cards.section: Stability: how to score it, and when cancelling fails

cards.front: What did Pennekamp and colleagues (2018) find in 690 aquatic ciliate microcosms about richness and stability?
cards.back: Richness raised temporal stability but lowered resistance to warming: stability measures can move in opposite directions.
cards.quote: in 690 aquatic ciliate microcosms, Pennekamp and colleagues (2018) found that richness raised temporal stability but lowered resistance to warming.
cards.section: Stability: how to score it, and when cancelling fails

cards.front: In the BEF-China planted forest, 16-species mixtures stored more than twice the carbon of the average monoculture after eight years. Why does the benchmark matter?
cards.back: Mixtures held more than twice the average monoculture's carbon but only an amount similar to two commercial monocultures, so the verdict depends on the benchmark.
cards.quote: 16-species mixtures had accumulated more than twice the carbon of the average monoculture after eight years, and an amount similar to two commercial monocultures.
cards.section: Beyond the plots

cards.front: A synthesis of 67 field studies finds positive biodiversity-biomass associations after adjusting for environmental covariates. How does this evidence differ from Cedar Creek's?
cards.back: Adjustment is not random assignment: an unmeasured variable could still drive both richness and biomass. Random assignment of richness rules that out within the experiment; the field synthesis extends the question to real systems.
cards.quote: Adjustment is not random assignment: an unmeasured variable could still drive both.
cards.section: Beyond the plots

cards.front: Grassland plots with more plant species have more biomass in a survey. Outline a field experiment to test whether richness causes the difference.
cards.back: Block a uniform field by soil and slope; randomly assign plots to 1, 2, 4 or 8 species, several random compositions per level plus every monoculture; constant area and seed mass; weed alike; check soil and light do not differ by treatment; analyse assigned richness with block as a factor.
cards.why: Assigning richness yourself breaks the link with soil fertility or moisture.
cards.quote: Divide a uniform field into blocks by soil and slope.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a richness experiment, why plant a monoculture of every species and harvest species separately each year?
cards.back: The Loreau-Hector partition needs each species' yield in mixture and in monoculture, so net, complementarity and selection effects can be computed year by year.
cards.quote: Treat the plot as the unit, harvest species separately each year for several years, and analyse assigned richness, with block as a factor.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Are uncorrelated species necessarily independent?
cards.back: No. Independent species are always uncorrelated, but uncorrelated species need not be independent. Variances add whenever swings are uncorrelated.
cards.quote: Independent species are always uncorrelated, but uncorrelated species need not be independent.
cards.section: Uncorrelated is not the same as independent

cards.front: Why do analyses disagree on whether averaging or compensatory dynamics steadies diverse grasslands?
cards.back: Synchrony patterns can reverse with the length of the time series, so the inferred mechanism depends on how long you watch.
cards.quote: synchrony patterns can reverse with the length of the time series, so the inferred mechanism depends on how long you watch.
cards.section: The mechanism debate

cards.front: Can a random-assembly richness experiment predict how much biomass a real grassland loses as its species go extinct?
cards.back: Not directly. The experiments compared communities assembled with fewer species; real extinctions are not random draws, so random assembly does not mimic the order of loss. They show what richness can do in the communities built.
cards.quote: Real extinctions are not random draws from a pool, so random assembly does not mimic the order in which species are lost in nature.
cards.section: Assembled is not the same as lost

cards.front: A diverse plot overyields strongly, but its species swing fully in step. Is its total guaranteed a higher μ/σ than the monocultures?
cards.back: No. Full synchrony removes the averaging gain, but μ/σ also rises with the mean, so overyielding can still raise it; the outcome depends on the species' sizes and swings.
cards.why: Cedar Creek credited averaging plus overyielding, not covariance effects.
cards.quote: the 16-species plots averaged 180 percent more biomass than monocultures, and a higher mean raises μ/σ
cards.section: Stability: how to score it, and when cancelling fails

cards.front: Diverse plots show higher μ/σ over ten years than species-poor plots. Does that show they will resist a drought better?
cards.back: No. Temporal stability, resistance and resilience are different measures that need not agree; in ciliate microcosms richness raised temporal stability but lowered resistance to warming.
cards.quote: "Steadier" means steady across years, not resisting one drought or recovering afterwards.
